question: How can I use an hybridization of ontology and machine learning for text summarization ?

sections.text: The integration of ontology and machine learning for text summarization is a promising approach that leverages the strengths of both methodologies. This report explores how these two paradigms can be combined to enhance text summarization processes, focusing on recent advancements and methodologies.

Ontology-based prompt tuning is a technique that enhances the quality and contextual relevance of text summaries. By combining this with abstractive text summarization, a novel framework can be developed to address the limitations of traditional summarization methods. This approach fine-tunes the summarization process, ensuring that the generated summaries are not only accurate but also contextually relevant to the domain [[1]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11850540/#:~:text=Ontology%2Dbased%2Dprompt%2Dtuning%20and,relevance%2Dof%2Dnews%2Darticle). Recent evaluations have shown significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, with notable increases in ROUGE scores and other metrics [[2]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11850540/#:~:text=Our%2Devaluation%2Dresults%2Ddemonstrate,as%2DBART%2C%2DBERT%2C%2Dand).

sections.text: The hybridization of ontology and machine learning involves using both techniques to summarize text effectively. This approach is particularly useful in domain-specific applications, such as crisis management, where ontology can help identify common ancestors of named entities and cluster texts into different types of crises [[3]](https://www.researchgate.net/post/How-can-I-use-an-hybridization-of-ontology-and-machine-learning-for-text-summarization#:~:text=my%2Dwork%2Dconsists%2Dof,ontology%2Dand%2Dmachine%2Dlearning). However, ontology-based methods often require manual construction and maintenance, which can be subjective and time-consuming [[4]](https://www.researchgate.net/post/How-can-I-use-an-hybridization-of%2Dontology%2Dand%2Dmachine%2Dlearning%2Dfor%2Dtext%2Dsummarization#:~:text=Automatic%2Dsummarization%2Dbased%2Don,considered%2Dbetter%2Dthan%2Dother). Despite these challenges, ontology summarization remains a valuable technique for understanding and reusing ontologies [[5]](https://www.researchgate.net/post/How%2Dcan%2DI%2Duse%2Dan%2Dhybridization%2Dof%2Dontology%2Dand%2Dmachine%2Dlearning%2Dfor%2Dtext%2Dsummarization#:~:text=Ontology%2Dsummarization%2Dhas%2Dbeen,a%2Dnew%2Dor%2Dsupplementing).

sections.text: A novel hybrid semantic document indexing technique, known as MLOntoSDI, combines machine learning with domain ontology to address information retrieval issues. This method uses neural word embeddings and external sources to learn document annotation from unstructured text documents [[6]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0360835222009287#:~:text=The%2Dproposed%2Dapproach%2Dused,text%2Ddocuments%2Dfrom%2Dscientific). By extracting key phrases and feeding them into a machine learning model, the technique identifies concepts in a text using word embeddings and computer science ontology [[7]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0360835222009287#:~:text=The%2Dproposed%2Dsolution%2Duses,them%2Dinto%2Dthe%2DML). This approach is particularly effective for domain-specific datasets, such as scientific literature [[8]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0360835222009287#:~:text=The%2Dproposed%2Dmethod%2Dassigned%2Dweights%2Dto%2Dconcepts).

sections.text:
# Report on Leading Methods for Learning Terrain Traversability Costs in Robotics

In the field of robotics, learning terrain traversability costs automatically from robot experience is crucial for enhancing autonomous navigation capabilities. This report synthesizes recent advancements and methodologies in this area, focusing on various approaches that leverage machine learning, sensor data, and simulation environments.

### 1. Deep Learning and Sensor Data Integration

Recent methods utilize deep learning techniques combined with sensor data to predict traversability costs. These approaches often employ visual and LiDAR data to segment and classify environments, which are then used to estimate traversability costs for different terrain classes. This process allows for the planning of safe routes tailored to the specific capabilities of the robot [[1]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0921889023001331#:~:text=Nowadays%2C%20this%20is%20typically,%5B5%5D%20or%20LiDAR%20data)[[2]](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.08187v1#:~:text=To%20address%20this%2C%20we,geometric%20information%20of%20the). By integrating proprioceptive information, these methods can quantify surface properties like roughness and bumpiness, enhancing the accuracy of traversability predictions [[3]](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.08187v1#:~:text=To%20quantify%20the%20surface,proprioceptive%20information%20for%20network).

question: What data structures are commonly used to solve the Range Minimum Query (RMQ) problem?

sections.text:
# Report on Data Structures for Solving the Range Minimum Query (RMQ) Problem

The Range Minimum Query (RMQ) problem is a fundamental problem in computer science, which involves finding the minimum value in a sub-array of a given array. This report explores various data structures commonly used to solve the RMQ problem, highlighting their complexities, advantages, and limitations.

## 1. Sparse Table

The Sparse Table is a popular data structure for solving the RMQ problem due to its efficient query time. It allows queries to be answered in constant time \(O(1)\) after a preprocessing step that takes \(O(N \log N)\) time and space [[1]](https://cp-algorithms.com/sequences/rmq.html#:~:text=Sparse%20Table%20%2D%20answers,data%20structure%2C%20excellent%20time)[[2]](https://www.topcoder.com/community/competitive-programming/tutorials/range-minimum-query-and-lowest-common-ancestor/#:~:text=Sparse%20Table%20%28ST%29)[[3]](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/range-minimum-query-for-static-array/#:~:text=The%20sparse%20table%20method,extra%20space%20O%28n%20Log). The Sparse Table is particularly useful for static arrays where updates are not required, as it precomputes the minimum for all subarrays of size \(2^j\) [[4]](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/range-minimum-query-for-static-array/#:~:text=The%20idea%20is%20to,from%200%20to%20Log).

## 2. Segment Tree

Segment Trees are versatile data structures that can handle dynamic arrays, allowing both queries and updates. They answer each query in \(O(\log N)\) time, with preprocessing also taking \(O(N)\) time [[5]](https://cp-algorithms.com/sequences/rmq.html#:~:text=Segment%20tree%20%2D%20answers,to%20the%20other%20data)[[6]](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/range-minimum-query-rmq-in-python/#:~:text=Range%20Minimum%20Query%20%28RMQ%29,to%20efficiently%20answer%20range)[[7]](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/range-minimum-query-for-static-array/#:~:text=Another%20approach%20is%20to%20use%20Segment). Segment Trees are more complex to implement compared to Sparse Tables but offer the advantage of supporting updates, making them suitable for dynamic scenarios [[8]](https://www.topcoder.com/community/competitive-programming/tutorials/range-minimum-query-and-lowest-common-ancestor/#:~:text=Segment).

## 3. Cartesian Tree

A Cartesian Tree is an optimal solution for RMQ, providing constant time \(O(1)\) query performance after linear time \(O(N)\) preprocessing [[9]](https://blog.yj0.se/2021/range_minimum_queries_problem/#:~:text=Optimal%20solution%3A%20Cartesian)[[10]](https://cp-algorithms.com/sequences/rmq.html#:~:text=%2D%20Cartesian%20Tree%20and,in%20%24O%281%29%24%2C%20preprocessing%20in). This structure is particularly efficient for offline queries, where all queries are known in advance. The Cartesian Tree is often used in conjunction with the Farach-Colton and Bender algorithm to achieve optimal complexity [[11]](https://blog.yj0.se/2021/range_minimum_queries_problem/#:~:text=Cartesian%20trees%20and)[[10]](https://cp-algorithms.com/sequences/rmq.html#:~:text=%2D%20Cartesian%20Tree%20and,in%20%24O%281%29%24%2C%20preprocessing%20in).

sections.text: Pre-training models for table-specific tasks involves using specialized datasets and methods to enhance the model's ability to understand and process tabular data. This report explores the datasets and methods used in pre-training models for table-specific tasks, drawing from recent research and developments in the field.

Recent advancements have seen the compilation of extensive pre-training corpora comprising diverse tables sourced from platforms like Kaggle. These datasets are crucial for acclimating models to the specificities of tabular data, allowing them to perform well across various tasks such as classification and regression [[1]](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.20208v7#:~:text=To%20achieve%20this%20objective%2C,format%20across%20approximately%20300). Additionally, TableInstruct, a large-scale instruction tuning dataset, includes 1.24 million tables with 2.6 million instances, representing a wide array of real-world table tasks [[2]](https://osu-nlp-group.github.io/TableLlama/#:~:text=TableInstruct%20is%20a%20large%2Dscale,tasks%20based%20on%2Dreal%2Dworld).

The development of models like TapTap, which pre-trains on real-world tabular data to generate high-quality synthetic tables, supports applications such as privacy protection and missing value imputation [[3]](https://openreview.net/forum?id=3gdG9upo7e#:~:text=After%2Dpre%2Dtraining%2Don%2Da,value%2Dimputation%2C%2Dand%2Dimbalanced). Domain-specific datasets, such as those used in financial or medical fields, further refine a model’s understanding and performance in specialized areas [[4]](https://kili-technology.com/large-language-models-llms/9-open-sourced-datasets-for-training-large-language-models#:~:text=Bloomberg%2Dtrained%2Da%2Dtransformer,of%2Dcarefully%2Dcurated%2Dfinancial)[[5]](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.14076v1#:~:text=This%2Dpaper%2Dfocuses%2Don,pretraining%2Dfor%2Dspecialized%2Dlanguage).

Open-source datasets like The Pile and C4 provide large-scale corpora that enhance a model's generalization capabilities across broader contexts [[6]](https://kili-technology.com/large-language-models-llms/9-open-sourced-datasets-for%2Dtraining%2Dlarge%2Dlanguage%2Dmodels#:~:text=The%2DPile%2Dis%2Dan,capability%2Dacross%2Da%2Dbroader). These datasets are often used in conjunction with domain-specific data to balance general language understanding with specialized knowledge [[7]](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.14076v1#:~:text=There%2Dare%2Dmany%2Dpublicly,as%2Dwell%2Das%2Ddomain%2Dspecific).

Innovative pre-training approaches have been developed to tailor large language models (LLMs) to tabular data. For instance, a straightforward yet innovative pre-training approach involves using a unified prompt template to amalgamate task-specific instructions with table content [[8]](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.20208v7#:~:text=We%2Dintroduce%2Dan%2Dstraightforward,the%2Dspecificities%2Dof%2Dtabular). This method helps models better understand and process tabular data.

The Mask-Then-Predict objective, mirroring the Masked Language Model (MLM) approach in natural language processing (NLP), is employed to enhance the model's ability to predict missing values in tables [[9]](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.20208v7#:~:text=To%2Dconduct%2Dpretraining%2C%2Dwe,of%2Drelationships%2Dwithin%2Dtable%2Drelated). This method is crucial for tasks like filling in missing table values and performing classification and regression [[10]](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.20208v7#:~:text=This%2Dsection%2Dexplores%2Dthe,zero%2Dshot%2Dand%2Din%2Dcontext).

Multi-task training phases are used to refine a model’s specialization, allowing it to perform well across various downstream tasks [[11]](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.20208v7#:~:text=Multi%2DTask%2DTraining%2Dfor%2DDownstream,specialization%2Dthrough%2Dmulti%2Dtask%2Dtraining). Fine-tuning, whether full or feature extraction, is employed to adapt pre-trained models to specific tasks, enhancing their performance while maintaining broad language understanding [[12]](https://www.goml.io/blog/best-practices-for-training-and-fine-tuning-large%2Dlanguage%2Dmodels#:~:text=Users%2Dcan%2Dmodify%2Dpre%2Dtrained,particular%2Djobs%2Dby%2Dfine%2Dtuning).

Models like TARTE transform tables into knowledge-enhanced vector representations, capturing semantics and facilitating subsequent learning with minimal additional cost [[13]](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.14415v1#:~:text=TARTE%2C%2Da%2Dfoundation%2Dmodel,the%2Dstring%2Dto%2Dcapture). This approach leverages broad pre-training to embed implicit priors that aid in a wide variety of tasks [[14]](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.14415v1#:~:text=TARTE%2Dbuilds%2Don%2Dthe,a%2Dwide%2Dvariety%2Dof).

The pre-training of models for table-specific tasks involves a combination of diverse datasets and innovative methods. By leveraging large-scale, domain-specific, and synthetic datasets, along with advanced pre-training techniques, models can be effectively trained to handle the complexities of tabular data. These advancements not only improve model performance but also expand the potential applications of LLMs in processing structured data.

question: What are the advantages and limitations of applying bias mitigation algorithms during pre-processing, training and inference stages of a model?

sections.text: Bias in machine learning (ML) models is a significant concern as it can lead to unfair outcomes, particularly affecting protected groups. Bias mitigation algorithms are designed to address these issues at various stages of the ML lifecycle: pre-processing, training (in-processing), and inference (post-processing). This report explores the advantages and limitations of applying bias mitigation algorithms at these stages.

### Advantages 1. **Improved Fairness in Input Data**: Pre-processing mechanisms aim to correct biases in the input data, ensuring that the data used to train ML models is more fairly distributed with respect to sensitive attributes [[1]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/artificial-intelligence/articles/10.3389/frai.2025.1520330/full#:~:text=Pre%2Dprocessing%20mechanisms%20attempt%20to,attribute%20information%20%28Feldman%20et). This can lead to models that are inherently less biased from the outset. 2. **Proxy Use for Sensitive Attributes**: When sensitive attribute data is unavailable, proxies based on other features can be used to infer these attributes, allowing for the application of bias mitigation methods [[2]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/artificial-intelligence/articles/10.3389/frai.2025.1520330/full#:~:text=The%20most%20studied%20approach,features%20in%20the%20training). This approach can enhance fairness without directly using sensitive data. ### Limitations 1. **Dependency on Sensitive Attribute Data**: Many bias mitigation algorithms require datasets containing sensitive attribute values to assess fairness [[3]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11924408/#:~:text=most%20bias%20mitigation%20algorithms,the%20fairness%20of%20the)[[4]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/artificial-intelligence/articles/10.3389/frai.2025.1520330/full#:~:text=most%20bias%20mitigation%20algorithms,the%20fairness%20of%20the). The absence of such data can limit the effectiveness of pre-processing methods. 2. **Accuracy of Inferred Attributes**: The effectiveness of bias mitigation methods can be significantly affected by the accuracy of inferred sensitive attributes [[5]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/artificial-intelligence/articles/10.3389/frai.2025.1520330/full#:~:text=The%20accuracy%20of%20the,of%20different%20bias%20mitigation). Inaccurate inferences can lead to suboptimal fairness outcomes.

question: What considerations are important for material selection in fabricating industrial robotic grippers?  What are the advantages and disadvantages of soft vs rigid gripper materials?

sections.text:
Introduction
The selection of materials for fabricating industrial robotic grippers is crucial for ensuring optimal performance, durability, and efficiency. This report explores the key considerations in material selection and compares the advantages and disadvantages of using soft versus rigid materials in robotic grippers.

Considerations for Material Selection

### Object Characteristics
The characteristics of the objects to be handled, such as size, mass, and material, are primary considerations in gripper design. The gripper must be capable of securely holding the object without causing damage [[1]](https://www.automationworld.com/factory/robotics/podcast/22458619/robot-gripper-selection-factors#:~:text=gripping%20always%20begins%20with,size%2C%20the%20mass%20and)[[2]](https://pactautomation.com/2023/03/06/grippers-types-materials-and-selection-criteria/#:~:text=The%20size%20and%20shape,securely%20and%20without%20causing). This requires a balance between gripping force and the delicacy of the object [[3]](https://pactautomation.com/2023/03/06/grippers-types-materials-and-selection-criteria/#:~:text=The%20gripping%20force%20is,that%20it%20damages%20the).

### Environmental Factors
The operating environment significantly influences material choice. Grippers may need to withstand extreme temperatures, contamination, or exposure to chemicals, which necessitates the use of materials that can endure such conditions [[4]](https://www.automationworld.com/factory/robotics/podcast/22458619/robot-gripper-selection-factors#:~:text=environmental%20factors.%20So%20once,to%20cleaning%20processes%20or)[[5]](https://pactautomation.com/2023/03/06/grippers-types-materials-and-selection-criteria/#:~:text=The%20environment%20in%20which,those%20used%20in%20cleanroom).

### Cost and Maintenance
Cost considerations include not only the initial investment but also ongoing maintenance and energy consumption. Materials that offer durability and low maintenance can reduce long-term costs [[6]](https://www.automationworld.com/factory/robotics/podcast/22458619/robot-gripper-selection-factors#:~:text=cost%2C%20of%20course%2C%20you,as%20well%20as%20energy).

### Precision and Control
The level of precision required in handling tasks dictates the choice of material. Mechanical grippers generally offer higher precision, while pneumatic and electric grippers provide varying levels of control and flexibility [[7]](https://www.automationworld.com/factory/robotics/podcast/22458619/robot-gripper-selection-factors#:~:text=Mechanical%20grippers%20generally%20offer,methods%20like%20vacuum%20and).

Soft vs. Rigid Gripper Materials

### Advantages of Soft Gripper Materials
Soft grippers, made from materials like silicone and elastomers, offer significant flexibility and adaptability. They can handle delicate objects without damage, making them ideal for applications in food handling and agriculture [[8]](https://www.automationworld.com/factory/robotics/podcast/22458619/robot-gripper-selection-factors#:~:text=Soft%20grippers%20like%20you,delicate%20objects%20without%20damaging)[[9]](https://soft-gripping.com/discover/soft-robotics-and-gripper-technology-for-object-recognition-and-handling/#:~:text=One%20of%20the%20advantages,more%20delicate%20manipulation%20of). Soft grippers can conform to complex shapes and surfaces, allowing for more delicate manipulation [[9]](https://soft-gripping.com/discover/soft-robotics-and-gripper-technology-for-object-recognition-and-handling/#:~:text=One%20of%20the%20advantages,more%20delicate%20manipulation%20of)[[10]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8125849/#:~:text=One%20of%20their%20most,soft%20objects%20without%20damaging). They are also safer for human interaction due to their gentle touch [[11]](https://builtin.com/articles/soft-robotics#:~:text=Soft%20robots%2C%20made%20from,tasks%20and%20direct%20human).

### Disadvantages of Soft Gripper Materials
Despite their advantages, soft grippers have limitations. They often cannot handle heavy loads or exert significant force compared to rigid grippers [[12]](https://builtin.com/articles/soft-robotics#:~:text=Soft%20robots%20often%20cannot,force%20compared%20to%20hard). The flexible materials can degrade over time, and achieving precise movements can be challenging [[13]](https://builtin.com/articles/soft-robotics#:~:text=Often%20inspired%20by%20biological,or%20twist%20without%20losing). Additionally, the fabrication of soft grippers can be complex and difficult to scale [[14]](https://builtin.com/articles/soft-robotics#:~:text=soft%20robots%20are%20made,specialized%20materials%20and%20customized).

### Advantages of Rigid Gripper Materials
Rigid grippers, typically made from materials like aluminum and stainless steel, offer strength and precision. They are suitable for tasks requiring high force and accuracy, such as in manufacturing and automotive industries [[15]](https://soft-gripping.com/discover/soft-robotics-vs-hard-robotics/#:~:text=Hard%20robotics%20is%20widely,precise%20movements%2C%20strength%2C%20and). These materials are durable and can withstand harsh environments, making them ideal for industrial applications [[16]](https://pactautomation.com/2023/03/06/grippers-types-materials-and-selection-criteria/#:~:text=Aluminium%20is%20a%20lightweight,and%20can%20withstand%20high).

### Disadvantages of Rigid Gripper Materials
Rigid grippers lack the flexibility of soft grippers, which limits their ability to handle delicate or irregularly shaped objects without causing damage [[17]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8125849/#:~:text=Traditional%20hard%20robotic%20grippers,object%20to%20not%20damage). They are also less adaptable to dynamic environments and require precise control mechanisms to function effectively [[18]](https://soft-gripping.com/discover/soft-robotics-vs-hard-robotics/#:~:text=Hard%20robotics%20is%20revolutionizing,driving%20automation%20and%20technological).

question: The Nyquist-Shannon theorem provides an upper bound for the sampling period when designing a Kalman filter. Leaving apart the computational cost, are there any other reasons, e.g., noise-related issues, to set a lower bound for the sampling period? And, if so, is there an optimal value between these bounds?

sections.text: The Nyquist-Shannon theorem is a fundamental principle in the field of signal processing and communications, which states that a continuous signal can be completely reconstructed from its samples if the sampling frequency is greater than twice the highest frequency of the signal (Nyquist, 1928; Shannon, 1949). When designing a Kalman filter, which is an algorithm that provides estimates of some unknown variables given the measurements observed over time, the sampling period is a critical parameter. While the Nyquist-Shannon theorem provides an upper bound for the sampling period, it is important to consider whether there are reasons to set a lower bound for the sampling period, particularly in the context of noise-related issues.

sections.text: Aliasing is a phenomenon that occurs when a signal is undersampled, resulting in high-frequency components of the signal being indistinguishable from lower-frequency components. In the context of a Kalman filter, undersampling can lead to incorrect estimations as the filter might attribute high-frequency noise to changes in the estimated variables (Brown & Hwang, 2012). Therefore, a lower bound on the sampling period is necessary to avoid aliasing. The characteristics of the noise affecting the system also play a role in determining the lower bound for the sampling period. If the noise is white and Gaussian, it is evenly spread across all frequencies, and the sampling period must be chosen to ensure that the noise does not dominate the signal in the frequency domain (Maybeck, 1979). In practice, this means that the sampling frequency should be high enough to capture the relevant signal characteristics without amplifying the noise. The stability and convergence of the Kalman filter are also affected by the sampling period. A very low sampling period (high sampling frequency) can lead to numerical instabilities due to the finite precision of computational resources, and it may also affect the convergence rate of the filter (Simon, 2006). Therefore, there is a trade-off between the need to sample fast enough to capture the dynamics of the system and the need to maintain numerical stability and ensure convergence of the filter.

sections.text: Determining an optimal value for the sampling period within the bounds set by the Nyquist-Shannon theorem and noise-related considerations is a complex task. It depends on the specific characteristics of the system being observed, the dynamics of the variables of interest, and the nature of the noise. In general, the optimal sampling period is one that balances the need to avoid aliasing, minimize the impact of noise, and ensure the stability and convergence of the Kalman filter (Grewal & Andrews, 2008).

question: What is the known evidence for pervasiveness of gaming of citation metrics like citation count and h-index?

sections.text: Citation metrics, such as citation count and h-index, are crucial in evaluating academic performance and influence. However, the manipulation of these metrics has become a significant concern in the academic community. This report explores the evidence of gaming citation metrics, highlighting various methods and their implications.

The manipulation of citation metrics often involves the fabrication of citations and the inflation of h-index scores. Platforms like Google Scholar and ResearchGate are exploited to create the illusion of a prolific research career. For instance, individuals can upload any PDF to ResearchGate, which Google Scholar then indexes as scholarly work, regardless of its credibility. This allows users to artificially inflate their h-index by continuously uploading documents stuffed with fake references [[1]](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/gaming-h-index-dark-side-google-scholar-researchgate-suneth-agampodi-6fy8c#:~:text=Academic%20fraud%20has%20reached,of%20an%20accomplished%20research). Such practices can make fake scholars appear more accomplished than legitimate researchers, potentially leading to undeserved promotions, grants, and awards [[2]](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/gaming-h-index-dark-side-google-scholar-researchgate-suneth-agampodi-6fy8c#:~:text=Fake%20scholars%20appear%20more%20accomplished%20than%20legitimate).

## Introduction
Schema matching is a critical task in data integration, involving the alignment of a source schema with a target schema to establish correspondence between their elements. This report explores the application of large language models (LLMs) in addressing the schema matching problem and evaluates their effectiveness.

## Application of Large Language Models in Schema Matching

### Automation and Semantic Recognition
Large language models (LLMs) have been applied to automate schema matching by leveraging both structural and natural language cues. This capability allows LLMs to recognize semantic similarities between schema elements, offering a potential solution to the complex problem of schema matching [[1]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250524716B/abstract#:~:text=large%20language%20models%20%28LLMs%29,structural%20and%20natural%20language)[[2]](https://medium.com/@shrinath.suresh/ai-powered-schema-mapping-95f596d31590#:~:text=LLMs%20possess%20the%20capacity,solution%20to%20this%20intricate). The use of LLMs in schema mapping has been explored in recent studies, highlighting their potential to generate schema mappings effectively [[3]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.24716#:~:text=Recent%20studies%20have%20explored,used%20to%20generate%20schema)[[4]](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2505.24716#:~:text=Recent%20studies%20have%20explored,used%20to%20generate%20schema).

### Practical Applications
LLMs have found practical applications in schema mapping across various industries, including healthcare, insurance, finance, and manufacturing. These models are particularly effective in domains where domain knowledge is crucial, as they can process natural language descriptions to enhance schema matching performance [[5]](https://medium.com/@shrinath.suresh/ai-powered-schema-mapping-95f596d31590#:~:text=Schema%20mapping%20finds%20practical,Care%2C%20Insurance%2C%20Finance%2C%20and)[[6]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.24716#:~:text=On%20the%20MIMIC%20dataset%2C,to%20process%20natural%20language).

### Novel Approaches and Techniques
Several novel methods have been developed to enhance schema matching using LLMs. For instance, the ReMatch method utilizes retrieval-enhanced LLMs, demonstrating effectiveness in real-world scenarios without the need for training data [[7]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240301567S/abstract#:~:text=In%20this%20paper%20we,retrieval%2Denhanced%20Large%20Language%20Models). Additionally, the Matchmaker program employs a compositional language model approach, which includes candidate generation, refinement, and confidence scoring, and has shown superior performance in medical schema matching benchmarks [[8]](https://openreview.net/forum?id=vR2MWaZ3MG#:~:text=Matchmaker%20%2D%20a%20compositional,generation%2C%20refinement%20and%20confidence).

### Comparative Performance
LLM-based methods have been compared with traditional string-similarity-based baselines, often outperforming them in various task scopes. For example, moving from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 has resulted in improved F1-scores due to increased precision and recall in different task scopes [[15]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.11852?#:~:text=Large%20Language%20Models%20%28LLMs%29,of%20tasks%2C%20including%20data). question: What are some practically-relevant properties of k-node subgraphs that can be counted in faster than cubic time in the size of the input graph?

sections.text:
## Introduction
Counting k-node subgraphs in graphs is a fundamental task in graph theory and has significant applications in various fields such as social network analysis, bioinformatics, and computer networks. The challenge lies in the combinatorial explosion of possibilities as the size of the graph increases. This report explores the properties of k-node subgraphs that can be counted in faster than cubic time, focusing on recent advancements and methodologies.

## Properties and Algorithms for Fast Counting

### 1. Clique Counting Algorithms
Clique counting is a crucial task in graph mining, with many applications across different domains. The task is algorithmically challenging due to the combinatorial explosion of possibilities as the size of the graph increases. However, several algorithms have been developed to address this challenge, focusing on counting k-cliques efficiently [[1]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11622928/#:~:text=Clique%20counting%20is%20a,crucial%20task%20in%20graph). The Bron–Kerbosch algorithm is a seminal method for identifying all maximal cliques within an undirected graph, and it has been foundational in developing more efficient algorithms [[2]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11622928/#:~:text=The%20Bron%E2%80%93Kerbosch%20algorithm%20%28Bron,cliques%20within%20an%20undirected). The ARBO algorithm introduces graphlet counting for various subgraphs, including cliques, using the arboricity concept, which can lead to faster counting times [[3]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11622928/#:~:text=The%20article%20ARBO%20%28Chiba,cliques%20using%20the%20arboricity).

### 2. Critical Subgraph Detection
Critical subgraphs, such as k-vertex-critical subgraphs (k-VCS), are subgraphs that maintain certain properties even when vertices are removed. Detecting these subgraphs can be done using various algorithms, such as the removal and insertion algorithms, which are designed to be efficient and can potentially operate in faster than cubic time [[4]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166218X07001096#:~:text=Given%20an%20integer%20k%2C,vertex%2Dcritical%20subgraph%20%2C%20such). The neighborhood weight heuristic and local search strategies have also been shown to be effective in finding smaller critical subgraphs, which can be counted more efficiently [[5]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166218X07001096#:~:text=The%20heuristic%20we%20now,smaller%20critical%20subgraphs%20of).

### 3. Subgraph Frequencies and Constraints
Subgraph frequencies describe a graph by the frequencies with which all possible small subgraphs occur within it. These frequencies are constrained by fundamental combinatorial properties, which can be leveraged to count subgraphs more efficiently [[6]](http://stanford.edu/~jugander/subgraphs/#:~:text=Subgraph%20frequencies%20describe%20a,graph%20by%20the%20frequencies). For instance, the frequencies of 3-node and 4-node subgraphs are constrained within specific simplices, which can reduce the computational complexity of counting these subgraphs [[7]](http://stanford.edu/~jugander/subgraphs/#:~:text=in%20a%204%2Dsimplex%20and%20an%2011%2Dsimplex%2C).

question: What are some of the challenges associated with creating a training dataset for question answering in scientific domains? Describe some recent methods that try to overcome these challenges.

sections.text:
## Introduction

Creating training datasets for question answering (QA) in scientific domains is a complex task fraught with challenges. These challenges stem from the unique characteristics of scientific literature, such as its specialized language, the rapid evolution of knowledge, and the need for high accuracy. This report outlines some of the primary challenges and describes recent methods developed to address these issues.

## Challenges in Creating Training Datasets for Scientific QA

### Specialized Language and Terminology

Scientific texts are replete with specialized terminology, jargon, and complex sentence structures, which can be difficult for natural language processing (NLP) systems to interpret. The precision of terms and the importance of context in scientific literature mean that QA systems must have a deep understanding of the domain to function effectively (Beltagy et al., 2019).

### Data Sparsity and Imbalanced Datasets

Scientific domains often suffer from data sparsity, where there are insufficient examples of certain phenomena to train robust models. Additionally, datasets may be imbalanced, with overrepresentation of some topics and underrepresentation of others, leading to biased models (Sun et al., 2017).

### Rapid Evolution of Knowledge

Scientific knowledge is constantly evolving, with new findings frequently rendering existing information outdated. This dynamism poses a challenge for QA datasets, which must be regularly updated to remain relevant and accurate (Riedel et al., 2013).

### High Standards for Accuracy

In scientific domains, the cost of misinformation can be high, necessitating extremely accurate QA systems. This requires high-quality, well-annotated datasets that are often expensive and time-consuming to create (Wang et al., 2018).

## Recent Methods to Overcome Challenges

### Pretrained Language Models

Recent approaches have leveraged pretrained language models that are fine-tuned on scientific texts. Models like SciBERT (Beltagy et al., 2019) are trained on large corpora of scientific literature to capture the domain-specific language and can then be fine-tuned on smaller, task-specific datasets.

### Data Augmentation Techniques

To combat data sparsity and imbalance, researchers have employed data augmentation techniques. These methods generate synthetic data by modifying existing data points or creating new ones based on the patterns learned from the original dataset (Wei & Zou, 2019).

### Continuous Learning and Updating

To address the rapid evolution of knowledge, some systems implement continuous learning strategies, where the model is regularly updated with new data. This can involve active learning, where the model identifies gaps in its knowledge and seeks out new information to fill those gaps (Settles, 2009).

### Expert-Informed Annotation

For high accuracy, expert-informed annotation processes are used. These involve domain experts who work alongside data annotators to ensure that the data is labeled correctly, thus improving the quality of the training dataset (Sabou et al., 2014).

Recent methods to overcome these challenges include the use of pretrained language models, data augmentation, continuous learning, and expert-informed annotation. Noise and outliers can significantly affect the quality of surface reconstruction. Noise reduction involves removing unwanted variations in the data, which can be achieved through techniques like median filtering to eliminate speckle or impulse noise [[1]](https://medium.com/@murtazasafri/point-cloud-data-0d8c8208e06f#:~:text=Median%20filtering%20is%20used,noise%2C%20%E2%80%9Cshot%E2%80%9D%20or%20impulse). Outlier removal is another critical step, where techniques such as Statistical Outlier Removal and Radius Outlier Removal are employed to discard points that deviate significantly from their neighbors [[2]](https://medium.com/@murtazasafri/point-cloud-data-0d8c8208e06f#:~:text=One%20such%20technique%20is,neighbors%20in%20a%20statistical). These steps are essential to enhance the quality of the point cloud and ensure that the reconstruction algorithms produce accurate results [[3]](https://medium.com/@rvtcadseo/best-techniques-of%20point-cloud-to-3d-28b82f0094ab#:~:text=Noise%20reduction%2C%20outlier%20removal%2C,quality%20of%20the%20point)[[4]](https://doc.cgal.org/latest/Manual/tuto_reconstruction.html#:~:text=Some%20acquisition%20techniques%20generate,far%20away%20from%20the).

## Downsampling

Point clouds often contain a large number of points, which can be computationally expensive to process. Downsampling reduces the dataset size while preserving essential features. Techniques such as Voxelization Grid downsampling and Uniform subsampling are commonly used. Voxelization involves creating a grid over the point cloud and averaging the points within each voxel, while Uniform subsampling selects every k-th point [[5]](https://medium.com/@murtazasafri/point-cloud-data-0d8c8208e06f#:~:text=In%20Voxelization%20Grid%20down,the%20points%20in%20the). These methods help in managing memory usage and processing time without compromising the data's integrity [[6]](https://medium.com/@murtazasafri/point-cloud-data-0d8c8208e06f#:~:text=Dense%20point%20clouds%20with,or%20subsample%20the%20point)[[7]](https://doc.cgal.org/latest/Manual/tuto_reconstruction.html#:~:text=CGAL%20provides%20several%20simplification%20algorithms).

question: How effective are language models at automatically generating textual descriptions of scientific concepts?

sections.text: Language models, particularly large language models (LLMs), have become increasingly prominent in the field of natural language processing (NLP). These models are designed to interpret and generate human-like text, making them valuable tools for various applications, including the generation of textual descriptions of scientific concepts. This report explores the effectiveness of LLMs in this domain, drawing on recent studies and findings.

### High-Quality Text Generation
LLMs have demonstrated the ability to generate high-quality text that is often indistinguishable from human-written content. This capability is crucial for tasks such as summarization, translation, and content creation, which are essential in scientific communication [[1]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10485814/#:~:text=A%20large%20language%20model,or%20questions%20%28Kasneci%20et)[[2]](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.12599v1#:~:text=Large%20Language%20Models%20%28LLMs%29,demonstrated%20high%20text%20generation). The models are trained on vast datasets, allowing them to learn linguistic patterns and generate coherent and contextually relevant text [[3]](https://www.contentserv.com/blog/automated-text-generation-is-powering-content-creation#:~:text=Language%20models%20trained%20on,and%20paragraphs%20with%20contextual).

### Consistency and Accuracy
Recent studies have shown that LLMs can achieve high levels of consistency and accuracy in generating scientific text. For instance, the LITURAt model achieved an internal consistency rate of 94.8% and an external consistency rate of 91.9% across repeated and rephrased queries [[4]](https://mental.jmir.org/2025/1/e68135#:~:text=LITURAt%20achieved%20an%20internal,across%20repeated%20and%20rephrased). Similarly, GPT-4 was rated 80.3% accurate and comprehensive in its responses, with a significant portion receiving the highest rating for completeness and precision [[5]](https://mental.jmir.org/2025/1/e68135#:~:text=3%25%20%28171/213%29%20of%20the,accurate%20and%20comprehensive%2C%20with).

### Application in Scientific Research
LLMs are revolutionizing the scientific research process by automating various stages, including hypothesis discovery, experimental design, and data analysis [[6]](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.04306v1#:~:text=LLMs%20are%20currently%20being,of%20the%20scientific%20research). They also contribute to scientific writing by generating citations, related work sections, and even drafting entire papers [[7]](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.04306v1#:~:text=We%20also%20cover%20their,and%20even%20drafting%20entire). This automation reduces the time and effort required for language editing and proofreading in academia [[8]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10485814/#:~:text=LLMs%20can%20be%20powerful,academia%20%28Pividori%20and%20Greene%2C).

sections.text:
### Resource Intensity
Despite their capabilities, LLMs require substantial computational resources and large-scale, high-quality datasets for training and inference [[9]](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.10729v1#:~:text=However%2C%20these%20LLMs%20face,inference%20cost%20OpenAI%20et). This resource intensity can be a barrier to their widespread adoption, particularly in resource-constrained environments [[10]](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.10729v1#:~:text=The%20lack%20of%20labeled,models%20in%20various%20scientific).

### Hallucination and Control
One of the challenges associated with LLMs is their propensity for hallucination, where the model generates text that is plausible but incorrect or nonsensical [[11]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877050925016576#:~:text=A%20survey%20on%20hallucination,taxonomy%2C%20challenges%2C%20and%20open). Techniques such as Controllable Text Generation (CTG) are being developed to ensure that outputs adhere to predefined control conditions, maintaining quality while avoiding hallucination [[12]](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.12599v1#:~:text=These%20varied%20demands%20have,of%20helpfulness%2C%20fluency%2C%20and).

### Domain-Specific Knowledge
Fine-tuning LLMs with domain-specific knowledge is essential to enhance their performance in specialized fields such as materials science [[13]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949747724000344#:~:text=Fine%2Dtuning%20of). This process allows models to provide more accurate and contextually relevant information, leveraging domain knowledge to improve predictive capabilities [[14]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41524-025-01554-0#:~:text=Models%20should%20be%20able,and%20provide%20contextually%20relevant).

question: What are the main challenges in adapting transformer-based models for tabular data representation?

sections.text: Transformer-based models have revolutionized fields like natural language processing and computer vision, but their adaptation to tabular data presents unique challenges. This report explores the main challenges faced in this adaptation process, drawing insights from recent research and developments.

Tabular data often contains heterogeneous data types and lacks inherent structure, making it difficult to synthesize and represent effectively using transformer models. This heterogeneity requires models to handle both categorical and numerical data efficiently, which is not straightforward with traditional transformer architectures designed for sequential data [[1]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0004370225000116#:~:text=Tabular%20data%20synthesis%20%28TDS%29,data%20and%20lack%20inherent).

question: In recommendation systems, how are new methods that optimize diversity typically evaluated?

sections.text:
# Evaluation of Diversity Optimization Methods in Recommendation Systems

In the realm of recommendation systems, optimizing for diversity is crucial to enhance user experience and engagement. This report explores how new methods that optimize diversity are typically evaluated, focusing on the metrics and methodologies used in recent research.

## Evaluation Metrics for Diversity

### Coverage and Effective Catalog Size

Coverage is a fundamental metric used to evaluate diversity in recommendation systems. It measures the proportion of unique items recommended out of the total available items, providing insight into how well the system exposes users to a wide range of content [[1]](https://shunya-vichaar.medium.com/diving-into-diversity-metrics-elevate-your-recommender-systems-in-a-snap-57637de380e1#:~:text=Coverage%20%28%25%29%20%3D%20%28Number,of%20Items%20Available%29%20%2A). For instance, a coverage of 20% indicates that 20% of the available items are being recommended [[2]](https://shunya-vichaar.medium.com/diving-into-diversity-metrics-elevate-your-recommender-systems-in-a-snap-57637de380e1#:~:text=Coverage%20%3D%20%282%2C000%20/,10%2C000%29%20%2A%20100%20%3D). Effective Catalog Size (ECS) is another metric that quantifies the number of items required to represent typical user activity, offering a more nuanced view of diversity in content consumption [[3]](https://shunya-vichaar.medium.com/diving-into-diversity-metrics-elevate-your-recommender-systems-in-a-snap-57637de380e1#:~:text=Effective%20Catalog%20Size).

### Diversity Indices

Diversity indices, such as the Gini-Simpson Diversity Index, are employed to quantify the dissimilarity among recommended items. This index helps in understanding the variety within a recommendation list, ensuring that users are not confined to a narrow set of options [[4]](https://shunya-vichaar.medium.com/diving-into-diversity-metrics-elevate-your-recommender-systems-in-a-snap-57637de380e1#:~:text=Gini%2DSimpson%20Diversity). Such metrics are crucial for preventing over-specialization and promoting user discovery [[5]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10762851/#:~:text=diverse%20and%20serendipitous%20recommendations,content%20and%20enhance%20user).

### Novelty and Serendipity

Novelty and serendipity are also critical components of diversity evaluation. Novelty measures the system's ability to introduce users to long-tail items, which are less popular but potentially interesting [[6]](https://neptune.ai/blog/recommender-systems-metrics#:~:text=It%20is%20a%20measure,introduce%20long%2Dtail%20items%20to). Serendipity, on the other hand, refers to the unexpectedness of recommendations, encouraging users to explore beyond their usual preferences [[7]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10762851/#:~:text=Serendipity%2C%20indicating%20the%20unexpected,usual%20preferences%20and%20stimulates)[[8]](https://milvus.io/ai-quick-reference/why-are-diversity-metrics-important-in-recommender-systems#:~:text=focusing%20solely%20on%20accuracy,limiting%20discovery%20of%20new).

sections.text:
## Methods for Enhancing and Evaluating Diversity

### Multi-objective Optimization

Multi-objective optimization frameworks, such as NewCrossPMOEA, are designed to balance precision and topic diversity, providing trade-off solutions that enhance both accuracy and diversity [[9]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0957417419305597#:~:text=A%20novel%20multi%2Dobjective%20recommendation,obtain%20trade%2Doff%20solutions%20%28recommendation). These frameworks often integrate with similarity models to achieve superior results in terms of diversity and novelty [[10]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0957417419305597#:~:text=The%20combination%20of%20NewCrossPMOEA,precision%20concerning%20the%20competing).

### Graph-based Approaches

Graph-based methods, like DGRec and DDGraph, utilize advanced techniques such as submodular neighbor selection and dynamic graph construction to capture diverse user-item interactions [[11]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10762851/#:~:text=The%20DGRec%20method%20diversifies,layer%20attention%2C%20and%20loss). These methods are evaluated using datasets like MovieLens and Netflix, demonstrating their effectiveness in enhancing diversity [[12]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.03030#:~:text=we%20validate%20the%20effectiveness,even%20some%20intent%2Daware%20diversity).

### Unified Metrics

Recent advancements propose unified metrics that combine topical diversity with accuracy, derived from search system evaluation metrics. These metrics are validated through experimental evaluations, ensuring they meet theoretical constraints and perform well in offline evaluations [[13]](https://research.google/pubs/towards-unified-metrics-for-accuracy-and-diversity-for-recommender-systems/#:~:text=We%20propose%20a%20novel,system%20evaluation%2C%20to%20Recommender).

sections.text:
## Importance of Diversity Metrics

Diversity metrics are essential for creating engaging, fair, and sustainable recommendation systems. They help in avoiding "filter bubbles," where users are only exposed to similar content, thus limiting their discovery of new items [[8]](https://milvus.io/ai-quick-reference/why-are-diversity-metrics-important-in-recommender-systems#:~:text=focusing%20solely%20on%20accuracy,limiting%20discovery%20of%20new). By tracking metrics like category distribution and item similarity scores, developers can adjust algorithms to balance relevance and novelty, promoting fairness and system robustness [[14]](https://milvus.io/ai-quick-reference/why-are-diversity-metrics-important-in-recommender-systems#:~:text=By%20tracking%20diversity%20metrics,to%20balance%20relevance%20and).

## Conclusion

Evaluating diversity in recommendation systems involves a combination of coverage, diversity indices, novelty, and serendipity metrics. Multi-objective optimization and graph-based methods are prominent approaches for enhancing diversity, with unified metrics providing a comprehensive evaluation framework. These metrics and methods ensure that recommendation systems remain engaging and equitable, ultimately improving user satisfaction and system performance.

question: How good are LLMs at solving traditional tabular ML datasets using ICL?

sections.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized various domains, particularly in natural language processing (NLP). However, their application to tabular data, a prevalent format in machine learning, remains a topic of active research. This report explores the capabilities of LLMs in solving traditional tabular machine learning (ML) datasets using in-context learning (ICL).

Despite their potential, LLMs face challenges when applied to tabular data due to its structured nature, which differs significantly from the unstructured data they are typically trained on [[5]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.17944#:~:text=Despite%20the%20impressive%20capabilities,in%20the%20inherent%20data)[[6]](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.17944v2#:~:text=Despite%20the%20impressive%20capabilities,in%20the%20inherent%20data).

# Report on Algorithms for Compressing Trees and Their Computational Complexity

Tree compression algorithms are essential in various fields, including data storage, image processing, and bioinformatics. This report compares different algorithms used for compressing trees, focusing on their computational complexity.

## 1. Compression-Complexity Measures

Compression-complexity measures such as Effort-to-Compress (ETC) and Lempel-Ziv Complexity (LZC) are used to analyze and classify genomic sequences. These measures provide an efficient alternative to standard methods for genome analysis, offering high classification accuracy and sensitivity [[1]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9857615/#:~:text=compression%2Dcomplexity%2D%28Effort%2Dto%2DCompress%2D%20or%2DETC,measures%2Dfor%2Danalyzing%2Dgenomic). These algorithms are particularly useful in bioinformatics for reproducing phylogenetic trees and classifying coronaviruses with high accuracy [[2]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9857615/#:~:text=The%2Dproposed%2Ddistance%2Dmeasure,and%2Dthose%2Dnot%2Dcausing).

question: How have open-source publishing platforms impacted the global distribution of academic publishing?

sections.text: Open-source publishing platforms have significantly transformed the landscape of academic publishing. This report explores how these platforms have influenced the global distribution of academic research, focusing on accessibility, cost, and the democratization of knowledge.

Open-source publishing platforms have enhanced global accessibility to academic research by minimizing costs associated with printing, distribution, and storage [[1]](https://publishingstate.com/open-access-revolution/2024/#:~:text=Online%20publishing%20platforms%20have,printing%2C%20distribution%2C%20and%20storage). This has allowed for more equitable access to knowledge, particularly benefiting researchers and students in developing countries who may not have institutional journal subscriptions [[2]](https://publishingstate.com/open-access-revolution/2024/#:~:text=More%20equitable%20access%20to,and%20students%20in%20developing). The rise of open-access journals and the transformation of subscription journals into open-access media have further facilitated the global distribution of scholarly works [[3]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3760666/#:~:text=open%2Daccess%20journals%20have%20appeared,fully%20or%20partially%20open%2Daccess)[[4]](https://www.libraries.rutgers.edu/research-support/copyright-guidance/copyright-academic-research-and-publication/scholarly-publishing-traditional-and-open-access#:~:text=The%20publishing%20landscape%20has,and%20distribution%20of%20scholarly).

sections.text: The integration of citation graphs with neural language models has become a significant area of research, particularly in enhancing the capabilities of these models in the context of scientific papers. This report explores how citation graphs are utilized to improve neural language models, focusing on various methodologies and their implications.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), particularly Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), have been effectively combined with text embeddings to recommend relevant academic papers. This approach involves building a citation graph of research papers, embedding each paper’s title and abstract, and using a GCN to learn powerful node representations. This method integrates local structural information from the citation graph, which is crucial for tasks like link prediction and node classification [[1]].

sections.text: IntroductionThe concept of fairness in machine learning (ML) is multifaceted, with numerous metrics proposed to evaluate and ensure fairness in models. This report explores how different fairness metrics correlate with each other across various datasets and model architectures. It also examines the challenges and considerations in selecting appropriate metrics for specific contexts.

Fairness Metrics OverviewFairness metrics in ML aim to ensure that models do not discriminate against individuals or groups based on sensitive attributes. Common metrics include demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity. Demographic parity ensures predictions are independent of sensitive group membership, while equalized odds require models to perform equally well across groups. Equal opportunity is a relaxed version of equalized odds, focusing only on positive outcomes [[1]](https://fairlearn.org/main/user_guide/assessment/common_fairness_metrics.html#:~:text=Demographic%20parity%20is%20a,membership%20in%20a%20sensitive).

question: How has literature discussed AI as a design material?

sections.text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has increasingly been discussed in literature as a transformative force in the design industry. This report synthesizes key points from recent literature to explore how AI is perceived and utilized as a design material, its impact on creativity, and the challenges it presents.

AI is increasingly recognized as a design material, offering designers new opportunities to innovate and enhance user experiences. This perspective is supported by the notion that AI, particularly machine learning, provides a compelling array of features that can be integrated into design processes to improve outcomes [[1]](https://medium.com/data-science/ai-as-design-material-2748d84bbb7b#:~:text=AI%2C%20and%20more%20specifically,is%20also%20a%20design). AI's role as a design material is not just about technological integration but also about rethinking design processes to incorporate AI's capabilities in recommendation, prediction, classification, clustering, and generation [[2]](https://medium.com/data-science/ai-as-design-material-2748d84bbb7b#:~:text=Clark%20details%20five%20ways,prediction%2C%20classification%2C%20clustering%2C%20and).

question: What are some biologically-inspired robot path planning algorithms?

sections.text: Biologically-inspired algorithms have become a significant area of research in robotics, particularly for path planning. These algorithms draw inspiration from natural processes and organisms to solve complex problems in robotics, such as navigation and obstacle avoidance. This report explores several biologically-inspired path planning algorithms, highlighting their mechanisms and applications.

One innovative approach to path planning is inspired by plant growth. This algorithm mimics the natural growth processes of plants, such as phototropism (growth towards light), negative geotropism (growth against gravity), and branching. These mechanisms are used to solve dynamic obstacle avoidance problems in unknown environments, particularly for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) [[1]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ChJAn..34i.199Z/abstract#:~:text=a%2Dbio%2Dinspired%2Dpath%2Dplanning%2Cin%2D3D%2Dspace%2Dis). The algorithm is noted for its fast path planning speed and the ability to plan paths with fewer route points, which is advantageous for real-time applications [[2]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ChJAn..34i.199Z/abstract#:~:text=the%2Dalgorithm%2Dhas%2Dthe%2Cspeed%2Dand%2Dfewer%2Droute). The feasibility of this approach has been verified through simulations and real-world experiments [[3]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ChJAn..34i.199Z/abstract#:~:text=feasibility%2Dof%2Dthe%2Dalgorithm%2CRobot%2DOperating%2DSystem%2D%28ROS%29).

question: how do post-quantum cryptography algorithms such as kyber/dilithium compare to corresponding non-quantum-safe methods in terms of performance and energy cost, and how could this be affected by future hardware optimizations?

sections.text: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is a field of cryptography that aims to develop cryptographic algorithms secure against the potential threats posed by quantum computers. This report focuses on two prominent PQC algorithms, Kyber and Dilithium, comparing them to traditional non-quantum-safe methods in terms of performance and energy cost. Additionally, the potential impact of future hardware optimizations on these algorithms is discussed.

### Kyber and Dilithium vs. Classical CryptographyKyber and Dilithium have been shown to achieve efficient execution times, often outperforming classical cryptographic schemes such as RSA and ECDSA at equivalent security levels. This is largely due to their reliance on lattice-based problems, which are computationally efficient to solve on classical hardware [[1]](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.12952v1#:~:text=Kyber%20and%20Dilithium%20achieve,ECDSA%20at%20equivalent%20security). Specifically, Kyber-768 can perform encryption in tens of thousands of CPU cycles or less with optimized code, which is faster than many classical methods like RSA [[2]](https://postquantum.com/post-quantum/nists-pqc-technical/#:~:text=Kyber%2D768%20encryption%20can%20be,classical%20RSA%20in%20many).### SPHINCS+ PerformanceSPHINCS+, another PQC algorithm, is a stateless hash-based digital signature scheme. However, it is generally slower and consumes more energy compared to lattice-based signatures like Dilithium [[3]](https://postquantum.com/post-quantum/nists-pqc-technical/#:~:text=SPHINCS%2B%20signatures%20are%20much,to%20generate%20than%20lattice%2Dbased)[[4]](https://medium.com/asecuritysite-when-bob-met-alice/energy-consumption-of-post-quantum-cryptography-dilithium-and-kyber-beat-our-existing-tls-1-3-ccadd04dd4c7#:~:text=Sphincs%2B%20key%20exchange%20method%2C,our%20traditional%20TLS%201.3). Despite its larger signature size and slower generation time, SPHINCS+ was chosen by NIST as a backup due to its different hardness assumptions [[5]](https://postquantum.com/post-quantum/nists-pqc-technical/#:~:text=SPHINCS%2B%20was%20chosen%20by,the%20lattice%2Dbased%20Dilithium%20and).

question: How does the tree covering technique differ in its application to ordinal trees versus binary trees?

sections.text:
## Introduction
Tree covering is a technique used in computer science to manage and optimize tree data structures. This report explores how tree covering techniques differ when applied to ordinal trees compared to binary trees. Ordinal trees and binary trees are both hierarchical data structures, but they have distinct characteristics and applications that influence how tree covering techniques are implemented.

### Succinct Representation
The tree covering technique for ordinal trees focuses on creating a succinct representation that supports all navigational operations while minimizing space requirements. This is achieved by using 2n + o(n) bits, which is efficient for handling large datasets [[1]](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-73420-8_45#:~:text=succinct%20representation%20of%20ordinal,only%202n%20%2B%20o(n)). This succinct representation is based on the work of Geary et al., and it allows for efficient level-order traversal, a feature that was previously limited in its application [[2]](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-73420-8_45#:~:text=supports%20efficient%20level%2Dorder%20traversal%2C,limited%20set%20of%20operations).

question: How are user demonstrations represented in domain-specific-language programs and used for automation tasks?

sections.text: Domain-Specific Languages (DSLs) are specialized languages tailored to specific application domains. They are particularly useful in automating tasks by representing user demonstrations and business processes in a structured and readable format. This report explores how DSLs are used to encapsulate user demonstrations and automate tasks, focusing on recent advancements and methodologies.

### Translating Business Processes
DSLs in test automation are designed to translate business processes into a readable and understandable format within test scripts. This approach shifts the focus from the technical implementation of an application to its functionality, making the tests more user-centric and aligned with business objectives [[1]](https://medium.com/@aydinserbest34/understanding-domain-specific-language-dsl-in-test-automation-focusing-on-business-logic-and-62fe9a79b1e6#:~:text=DSL%20in%20test%20automation,understandable%20format%20within%20test). By encapsulating the essence of the user

### Abstracting Technical Details
DSLs abstract away lower-level technical details, such as specific WebDriver commands, allowing test scripts to focus on business logic rather than technical validations [[3]](https://medium.com/@aydinserbest34/understanding-domain-specific-language-dsl-in-test-automation-focusing-on-business-logic-and-62fe9a79b1e6#:~:text=DSL%20hides%20lower%2Dlevel%20technical,such%20as%20specific%20WebDriver). This abstraction is complemented by the Page Object Model (POM), which encapsulates page-specific actions and elements, further simplifying the representation of user interactions [[4]](https://medium.com/@aydinserbest34/understanding-domain-specific-language-dsl-in-test-automation-focusing-on-business-logic-and-62fe9a79b1e6#:~:text=Page%20Object%20Model%20%28POM%29,encapsulating%20page%2Dspecific%20actions%20and).

### Automation of DSL Design
The AutoDSL framework represents a significant advancement in automating the design of DSLs. It automates the creation of DSL-based constraints across various domains, optimizing syntactic constraints and abstracting semantic constraints [[5]](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.659/#:~:text=we%20introduce%20the%20AutoDSL,constraint%20design%20across%20various). This automation reduces the labor-intensive efforts traditionally required for DSL design, making it more efficient and scalable [[6]](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.659/#:~:text=Domain%2Dspecific%20Language%20%28DSL%29%2C%20as%20an%20effective%20tool%20to%20express%20constraints%20structurally%2C%20often%20requires%20case%2Dby%2Dcase%20hand%2Dcrafting%2C%20necessitating%20customized%2C%20labor%2Dintensive%20efforts).

sections.text:
### Enhancing Procedural Planning
DSLs are used to accurately represent procedures in restricted scenarios, such as non-standardized scientific experiments, by precisely depicting constraints [[7]](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.659/#:~:text=Accurate%20representation%20of%20procedures,requires%20precise%20depiction%20of). The AutoDSL framework enhances procedural planning and execution by providing a structural representation of these constraints, which is crucial for maintaining the integrity of domain-specific tasks [[8]](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.659/#:~:text=Quantitative%20and%20qualitative%20analyses,improve%20procedural%20planning%20and).

### Integration with Language Models
The integration of DSLs with language models, as demonstrated by AutoDSL, highlights their potential as auxiliary modules for improving procedural planning and execution [[8]](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.659/#:~:text=Quantitative%20and%20qualitative%20analyses,improve%20procedural%20planning%20and). This integration allows for a more comprehensive approach to task automation, leveraging the strengths of both DSLs and language models [[9]](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.659/#:~:text=AutoDSL%3A%20Automated%20domain%2Dspecific%20language%20design%20for%20structural%20representation%20of%20procedures%20with%20constraints).

### Evaluation and Performance
Quantitative and qualitative analyses of DSLs designed by AutoDSL show their superiority over manually crafted solutions like BioCoder in terms of various metrics [[10]](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.12324v1#:~:text=The%20quantitative%20evaluation%20underscores,terms%20of%20four%20quantitative). The framework's ability to generalize DSL-based constraints across diverse domains underscores its effectiveness in automating domain-specific tasks [[11]](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.12324v1#:~:text=AutoDSL%20is%20capable%20of,design%20and%20domain%20expertise).

question: What are the leading techniques for person-following robot navigation (which must track the person and potentially re-identify if occluded)?

sections.text: Person-following robots are designed to autonomously follow a person, often for applications such as assistance robots, load-carrying robots, or companionship robots. Effective navigation is crucial for these robots, especially in dynamic environments where occlusions and interactions with other people or objects may occur. This report outlines the leading techniques for person-following robot navigation, focusing on tracking and re-identification when the target person is occluded.

Lidar sensors and depth cameras are commonly used for person-following robots. These sensors provide 3D information about the environment, which is useful for detecting and tracking a person. Robots can use this data to maintain a safe distance and navigate around obstacles while following a person (Wang et al., 2020).

Machine learning techniques, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), are often employed to improve the accuracy of visual tracking (Zhang et al., 2019).

question: how can RRT-based path planning be adapted to efficiently handle narrow pathways

sections.text:
# Adapting RRT-Based Path Planning for Narrow Pathways

Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) algorithms are widely used in path planning due to their ability to efficiently explore high-dimensional spaces. However, their performance can be challenged in environments with narrow pathways. This report explores various adaptations of RRT-based path planning to efficiently handle narrow pathways.

AI-RRT* is an advanced version of the RRT* algorithm that is particularly effective in narrow passages. It achieves asymptotic optimality with reduced computational time and shorter path lengths by using a hybrid sampler that leverages prior knowledge of narrow passages [[1]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12555-022-0834-9#:~:text=adaptive%20informed%20RRT%2A%20%28AI%2DRRT%2A%29%2C,and%20a%20shorter%20path). The algorithm also employs an adaptive tree growth strategy to determine the necessity of additional trees, enhancing its efficiency in complex environments [[2]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12555-022-0834-9#:~:text=an%20adaptive%20tree%20growth,necessity%20of%20a%20third). Simulation results demonstrate that AI-RRT* outperforms other sampling-based planners in terms of computation time, path length, and stability, making it highly suitable for narrow pathways [[3]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12555-022-0834-9#:~:text=the%20simulation%20results%20confirm,optimal%20solution%20in%20narrow).

sections.text: Introduction The Boolean Satisfiability Problem (SAT) is a fundamental problem in computational complexity theory and has significant applications across various fields such as computer science, artificial intelligence, and cryptography. The problem involves determining whether there exists an assignment of variables that satisfies a given Boolean formula [[1]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18778#:~:text=The%20Boolean%20Satisfiability%20Problem,Boolean%20formula%2C%20rendering%20it)[[2]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44335-025-00020-w#:~:text=Solving%20a%20SAT%20problem,that%20satisfies%20the%20CNF). Generating hard instances of SAT is crucial for testing the efficiency and robustness of SAT solvers, which are essential tools in solving complex computational problems [[3]](https://cacm.acm.org/research/the-silent-revolution-of-sat/#:~:text=Propositional%20Satisfiability%20%28SAT%29%20has,hard%20computational%20problems%20in).

sections.text: Leading Methods for Generating Hard SAT Instances ### 1. Digital Memcomputing Machines (DMMs) Digital Memcomputing Machines (DMMs) are a novel approach to solving SAT problems by leveraging non-linear dynamical systems. These machines are designed to solve constraint satisfaction problems, such as 3-SAT, with the assistance of memory. The continuous time dynamics of DMMs allow for efficient solution searches without resorting to chaotic dynamics, which is a significant advantage over traditional methods [[4]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-76666-2#:~:text=Here%2C%20we%20introduce%20a,both%20complete%20and%20incomplete). The scalability of DMMs is demonstrated through power-law scalability for typical 3-SAT instances, which traditionally require exponential time to solve [[5]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-76666-2#:~:text=Along%20with%20arguments%20for,to%20solve%20with%20successful). **Strengths**: DMMs offer polynomially-bounded scalability and efficient simulations, making them suitable for solving hard SAT instances [[4]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-76666-2#:~:text=Here%2C%20we%20introduce%20a,both%20complete%20and%20incomplete). **Weaknesses**: The approach is relatively new and may require further validation and optimization for broader applications [[6]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-76666-2#:~:text=NP%20question%2C%20they%20show,research%20in%20constraint%20satisfaction). ### 2. Deep Learning-Based SAT Generation Recent advancements have introduced deep learning methods to generate more realistic SAT instances. These methods aim to preserve the hardness of the original instances while generating them in a reasonable time frame [[7]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18778#:~:text=Recently%2C%20deep%2Dlearning%20methods%20have,generate%20more%20realistic%20SAT). The augmentation process has been shown to improve solver runtime prediction significantly, reducing mean absolute error by 20-50% on example datasets [[8]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18778#:~:text=We%20illustrate%20the%20value,absolute%20error%20by%2020%2D50). **Strengths**: Deep learning methods can generate realistic and hard SAT instances efficiently, enhancing the testing and development of SAT solvers [[9]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18778#:~:text=We%20propose%20a%20novel,in%20a%20reasonable%20time). **Weaknesses**: The reliance on deep learning models may introduce complexity and require substantial computational resources for training and inference [[7]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18778#:~:text=Recently%2C%20deep%2Dlearning%20methods%20have,generate%20more%20realistic%20SAT). ### 3. Graph Neural Network (GNN)-Based Core Detection A novel method involves using graph neural networks (GNNs) to detect the core of a SAT problem, which is a subset of clauses that are minimally unsatisfiable. This method iteratively refines the SAT instance using a GNN-based core detection procedure, preserving the hardness of the problem [[10]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18778#:~:text=Given%20an%20unsatisfiable%20%28UNSAT%29,Subset%20%28MUS%29%20or%20a). **Strengths**: The GNN-based approach is fast and effective in preserving the hardness of SAT instances, making it suitable for generating challenging test cases [[11]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18778#:~:text=We%20introduce%20a%20fast,uses%20a%20graph%20neural). **Weaknesses**: The method's effectiveness depends on the quality of the GNN model, which may require extensive training and tuning [[12]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18778#:~:text=We%20train%20a%20graph,network%20to%20perform%20the). ### 4. Partitioning and Metaheuristic Algorithms Partitioning approaches decompose a SAT instance into a family of independent instances, which can be solved separately. Metaheuristic algorithms, such as simulated annealing and tabu search, are used to explore the search space efficiently [[13]](https://springerplus.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s40064-016-2187-4#:~:text=In%20this%20paper%20we,the%20Boolean%20satisfiability%20problem). These methods are particularly useful for generating hard variants of SAT problems [[13]](https://springerplus.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s40064-016-2187-4#:~:text=In%20this%20paper%20we,the%20Boolean%20satisfiability%20problem). **Strengths**: Partitioning and metaheuristic algorithms can efficiently explore large search spaces and generate hard SAT instances [[14]](https://springerplus.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s40064-016-2187-4#:~:text=We%20use%20metaheuristic%20algorithms,point%20in%20the%20search). **Weaknesses**: The effectiveness of these methods is highly dependent on the chosen partitioning strategy and the specific metaheuristic algorithm used [[15]](https://springerplus.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s40064-016-2187-4#:~:text=The%20problem%20of%20search,optimization%20of%20the%20predictive).

question: What datasets and methods are used to pre-train models on table specific tasks?

sections.text: Pre-training models for table-specific tasks involves using specialized datasets and methods to enhance the model's ability to understand and process tabular data. This report explores the datasets and methods used in pre-training models for table-specific tasks, highlighting recent advancements and practices.

### General Datasets 1. **Common Crawl and C4**: The Common Crawl dataset, comprising terabytes of raw web data, is a foundational dataset for pre-training large language models (LLMs). C4, derived from Common Crawl, is a 750 GB English corpus specifically designed for LLM pre-training, emphasizing the importance of large-scale, clean data for model training [[1]](https://kili-technology.com/large-language-models-llms/9-open-sourced-datasets-for-training-large-language-models#:~:text=Common%20Crawl%20dataset%20comprises,from%20billions%20of%20web)[[2]](https://medium.com/@jelkhoury880/how-have-pre-training-datasets-for-large-language-models-evolved-13d74c01f8e8#:~:text=C4%2C%20created%20from%20CommonCrawl,for%2Dtraining%20large%20language). 2. **The Pile**: This is an 800 GB corpus that enhances a model’s generalization capability across a broader context, making it suitable for diverse applications, including table-specific tasks [[3]](https://kili-technology.com/large-language-models-llms/9-open-sourced-datasets-for-training-large-language-models#:~:text=The%20Pile%20is%20an,capability%20across%20a%20broader). 3. **ROOTS and Wikipedia**: ROOTS is a 1.6TB multilingual dataset, while the Wikipedia dataset provides cleaned text data in multiple languages, both contributing to the multilingual and diverse data needs of LLMs [[4]](https://kili-technology.com/large-language-models-llms/9-open-sourced-datasets-for-training-large-language-models#:~:text=ROOTS%20is%20a%201.6TB,text%20sourced%20in%2059). ### Table-Specific Datasets 1. **TableInstruct**: A large-scale instruction tuning dataset, TableInstruct includes 14 datasets with 11 tasks, curated from 1.24 million tables. It is designed to cover a variety of real-world table tasks, providing a comprehensive resource for training models on table-specific applications [[5]](https://osu-nlp-group.github.io/TableLlama/#:~:text=TableInstruct%20is%20a%20large%2Dscale,tasks%20based%20on%20real%2Dworld). 2. **Kaggle Tables**: An extensive pretraining corpus comprising diverse tables sourced primarily from Kaggle has been compiled to address the challenges LLMs face with structured tabular data [[6]](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.20208v7#:~:text=To%20achieve%20this%20objective%2C,format%20across%20approximately%20300). 3. **TapTap**: This dataset involves pre-training on a large corpus of real-world tabular data, enabling the generation of high-quality synthetic tables for various applications, including privacy protection and missing value imputation [[7]](https://openreview.net/forum?id=3gdG9upo7e#:~:text=In%20this%20paper%2C%20we,empower%20models%20for%20tabular).
